title: Physics XI — Academic Companion
subtitle: Twenty-six unit briefs that connect NEB Class 11 Physics to the working edge of the subject: what the model asserts, the conditions under which it holds, the questions that are still open, and where to read further.

units.summary: Before any law can be applied, a measurement has to be given a number, a unit, a direction where it matters, and an uncertainty. This unit fixes that vocabulary, and the 2019 SI redefinition moved the definition of the kilogram from a physical artefact to a fixed number.
facts: A physical quantity is a number multiplied by a unit; the unit is part of the quantity, not a label attached to it.
The SI defines seven base units (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd); every other unit is derived from them by definition, so the unit system is a language in which equations must be well-formed.
Since the 2019 redefinition the metre is fixed by c = 299 792 458 m/s exactly, the kilogram by the Planck constant h = 6.62607015e-34 J s exactly, and the kelvin by k = 1.380649e-23 J/K exactly.
Addition and subtraction demand matching dimensions; multiplication and division create new dimensions, which is why dimensional analysis can reject an equation before you compute anything.
Every measurement carries uncertainty: the final reported digit is uncertain, and the honest form of a result is best estimate plus or minus a bound.
Order-of-magnitude estimation (10^n) is a cheap sanity check: if the answer of a units question is 10^40, something has already gone wrong.

Dimensional homogeneity is a consistency test rather than a proof: an equation can be dimensionally perfect and still be wrong by a factor of two, a wrong sign, or an unaccounted dimensionless constant.
conditions: Dimensional analysis only proves that an equation is dimensionally consistent, never that it is right; dimensionless constants such as pi, G and friction coefficients are invisible to the check.
The 'linear law' shape of Hooke's law is dimensionally consistent but only valid inside a small-strain regime, which is exactly the regime students assume without checking.
The modern kilogram is realised with Kibble and watt balances, so old textbooks that describe a platinum-iridium cylinder under lock and key are describing a definition that no longer holds.
Percentage errors are meaningful only for quantities measured on a ratio scale; a percentage change in temperature measured in Celsius is not comparable to the same change in kelvin.

The seven SI base units are a convention, not a discovery - a different set of definitions would describe the same physics, which is exactly why the 2019 redefinition changed the artefacts without changing a single law.

mysteries.question: How small can the uncertainty of a realised kilogram become before metrology, rather than physics, sets the limit?
mysteries.note: Quantum metrology keeps tightening traceability, but no fundamental floor on repeated mass comparison has been identified.

mysteries.question: Should the SI keep seven base units, or fold constants such as the Boltzmann constant into a smaller set?
mysteries.note: The BIPM keeps this under periodic review; the debate is about definitional economy, not about new physics.

prompts: Express the speed of light, the Planck constant and the Boltzmann constant in base SI units and check that each is dimensionally M^0 L^0 T^0 Theta^0.
Your calculator reports g = 9.8 m/s^2. How many digits of that answer are trustworthy, and how would you justify your choice from the measurement alone?
Design a dimensional check that catches the classic mistake of adding a mass to a force.

keyNumbers.label: Number of SI base units
keyNumbers.value: 7 (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd)

units.summary: Vectors are the bookkeeping that lets a physical law stay true no matter how you choose to look at the situation. The unit is about representation: when a scalar law becomes a vector law, and which errors in representation produce wrong answers that still look plausible.
facts: A vector needs both magnitude and direction; two vectors of equal magnitude pointing in different directions are different vectors, unlike scalars.
Two vectors are equal only when they have identical magnitude and direction, regardless of the path taken to produce them, which is the formal statement of the principle of transmissibility.
Components are projections onto a chosen orthonormal frame; the frame is free to choose, but the numerical answer changes with the choice even though the physics does not.

The dot product A.B = AB cos(theta) is a scalar measuring alignment; the cross product magnitude |A x B| = AB sin(theta) is a scalar measuring perpendicularity, and the vector A x B is axial (a pseudovector).
Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum are vectors; speed, energy, temperature, mass and power are scalars.
Vector addition is commutative and associative, so the order in which forces are added cannot change the result - only the arithmetic errors can.
A vector needs three independent components in three dimensions, so a two-dimensional diagram silently drops one - the component the page cannot show is exactly the one a cross product uses.
conditions: Component arithmetic is valid only inside a single orthonormal frame; mixing components taken from different frames produces a number with no meaning.
The cross product obeys the right-hand rule and is anti-commutative: A x B = -(B x A), so the order of the operands matters even though the magnitudes are equal.
Two drawn vectors of equal length that look perpendicular on paper are not perpendicular if the page is scaled unevenly; always check magnitude and direction numerically.

Adding forces that act on different bodies is a category error: Newton's third-law pairs cancel in the total but each acts on something else, so they cannot be merged into one resultant on one object.
The cross product is defined only in three dimensions, so the planar perpendicular you draw is a construction convention rather than a coordinate-independent operation.

mysteries.question: Why does the quantum description of angular momentum look so different from the classical spinning-top picture?
mysteries.note: Spin is not a literal rotation of a rigid body: it has no defined axis in the classical sense, yet behaves like an angular momentum with quantum numbers.

mysteries.question: How does the quantum state of a spin-1/2 particle relate to the classical picture of a spinning top, if at all?
mysteries.note: The correspondence is suggestive but not exact: quantum angular momentum has no fixed axis, and the 1924 Stern-Gerlach experiment is still the cleanest experimental statement of the mismatch.

prompts: Resolve a 30 N force applied at 40 degrees to the horizontal into components, then find the resultant with a second 20 N force at 120 degrees.
Find the angle between two vectors of equal magnitude whose sum and difference happen to have the same magnitude, and interpret the result.
Verify a x (b x c) = b(a.c) - c(a.b) with components, then use it to find the rotation axis of a rigid body.

keyNumbers.label: Resultant of two equal vectors at 120 degrees
Components of a unit vector at 30 degrees to the x-axis
Magnitude of the sum of two unit vectors at 90 degrees

units.summary: Kinematics describes how things move without saying why. Its power is the graph: a position-time graph carries velocity, acceleration and everything else inside it, and the constant-acceleration formulas are only a special case of what the graph can show.
facts: Kinematics is the description of motion; dynamics is the explanation of motion. Newton's laws belong to the second half of the story.
v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at^2 and v^2 = u^2 + 2as all assume constant acceleration over the interval considered.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, not of speed: a body moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating continuously.
On a position-time graph the slope is velocity, the curvature is acceleration; the area under a velocity-time graph is displacement.
Near the Earth's surface a body in free fall accelerates at g = 9.8 m/s^2 downward, and the independence from mass holds only when air resistance is negligible.
The choice of sign convention (up positive or down positive) is a free decision; the physics is unchanged, but the arithmetic changes if you are inconsistent.
The three equations of motion are not three independent laws: they are one kinematic constraint written three ways, and they hold only for constant acceleration.
conditions: The constant-acceleration formulas fail for air drag, terminal velocity, appreciable changes in g with altitude, and charged particles in fields.
A vertical throw and a free fall from rest have identical acceleration-time graphs even though their velocity graphs differ - a standard examination trap.
Average velocity over a closed round trip is zero while the average speed is not, because the average of a vector quantity is not the average of its magnitude.
Projectile motion ignores the Earth's curvature and rotation; those corrections matter for long-range artillery and for orbital projectiles, not for a 10 m throw.
Each equation of motion throws away the shape of the velocity-time graph, so two motions with the same initial and final velocity can still be different - the acceleration history is what gets lost.

mysteries.question: How precisely can the equivalence of free fall be tested as the mass of the test body is reduced?
mysteries.note: Drop-tower and lunar/planetary drop experiments push the test to ever smaller masses; any quantum-gravity signal would appear as a deviation from the predicted free-fall trajectory.

mysteries.question: Does a trajectory carry more information than any observer can extract from it, given that measuring position disturbs the motion?
mysteries.note: Quantum limits on phase-space resolution remain an active research topic, and the classical description hides the disturbance entirely.

prompts: Derive v^2 = u^2 + 2as from the definition of average velocity, stating at each step where constant acceleration was used.
Sketch x-t, v-t and a-t graphs for a ball thrown vertically upward and mark every sign change.
A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes to rest in 2.5 s: find the retardation, then the reaction distance needed to avoid a collision.

keyNumbers.label: Typical terminal speed of a skydiver
Speed of sound in air at 20 degrees C

units.summary: Dynamics supplies the causes. Newton's three laws are the whole of classical mechanics for point masses, but the ways they are applied - free-body diagrams, variable mass, self-adjusting friction - decide whether an answer survives contact with reality.
facts: The first law defines an inertial frame: one in which a free body keeps constant velocity, and the second law then reads F = ma.
F = ma is the constant-mass form. For a changing mass the correct statement is F = dp/dt, which is what lets a rocket accelerate.
Third-law pairs act on different bodies, are equal and opposite, and share the same line of interaction.
Mass measures inertia and is independent of g; weight is the gravitational force mg, so weight changes with location while mass does not.
A free-body diagram isolates one body and contains only interactions, never 'forces of motion'.
Static friction is self-adjusting, 0 <= f <= mu N; only at impending slip does it reach mu N, which is why pulling a box at constant speed needs less force than starting it.
Newton's second law is a rate law: the force at an instant fixes the change of momentum, so a larger force acting for a shorter time can deliver exactly the same impulse.
conditions: F = ma assumes constant mass in an inertial frame; rockets, raindrops gaining mass from vapour, and chains picking up links all violate it.
Textbook problems neglect air resistance and buoyancy; both become dominant for light bodies, fine dust and falling feathers.

The classic 'lift and the Earth' third-law discussion fails because the force on the person and the force on the ground are not a third-law pair: the true partner of the person-Newton force is the person-Earth force.
Friction coefficients are empirical, depend on surface condition, cleanliness, humidity and sliding speed, and are not universal constants of the two materials.
Newton's laws assume an inertial frame and classical, instantaneous action; they hold to about one part in 10^10 of the speed of light and stop being fundamental at relativistic and quantum scales.

mysteries.question: Do smooth, globally defined solutions of the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations exist and remain smooth?
mysteries.note: The Clay Mathematics Institute announced an apparent solution in September 2026 and states that the work is still to be analysed and evaluated; it should be presented as announced, not as settled.

mysteries.question: Can the transition from laminar to turbulent flow be predicted from first principles?
mysteries.note: Direct numerical simulation still reaches only moderate Reynolds numbers, so the transition statistics remain an active research target.

prompts: Draw free-body diagrams for a lift accelerating upward with total mass m and explain both readings of the word 'weight'.
Show that the third law does not prevent a rocket from accelerating: track the momentum carried away by the exhaust.
Estimate the terminal velocity of a raindrop using a quadratic drag law and compare the estimate with observation.

keyNumbers.label: Force needed to accelerate 1 kg at 1 g
Impulse of a car decelerating from 50 m/s in 0.05 s
keyNumbers.value: about 250 N s per kg of mass

units.summary: Energy is the bookkeeping device that survives every form of friction. The work-energy theorem is the most useful sentence in mechanics: it replaces a force problem with an energy problem, and it stays valid even when the forces themselves are hard to compute.
facts: Work done by a constant force is the scalar product W = F.s.cos(theta); only the component of the force along the displacement contributes.
The work-energy theorem states that the net work on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy, dK = W_net, whatever the forces turn out to be.
A conservative force depends on position only; for it a potential energy exists with W = -dU, and the closed-path integral of the force vanishes.
Near the Earth's surface gravity is conservative with U = m g h; the spring force is conservative with U = (1/2) k x^2.
Mechanical energy conservation (K + U constant) holds only when no non-conservative work (friction, drag, driving) is done.
Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = dW/dt, and for a constant force P = F.v, so a bicycle climbs steeply not because it does more work but because it does it faster.

Work is a path-independent energy transfer only for conservative forces; friction turns ordered mechanical energy into disordered thermal energy, which is why the work-energy theorem has to carry a friction term.
conditions: Energy conservation is bookkeeping, not a claim that energy disappears: friction converts mechanical energy into internal energy and heats both surfaces.
Non-conservative forces cannot be described by a potential and must be handled through the work-energy theorem directly.
The constant-g potential m g h is a local approximation; the exact field potential is -GMm/r, and the two agree only for heights small compared with Earth's radius.
Efficiency is always defined against a specific output, can never exceed 1, and for most machines falls as the load rises because friction grows faster than useful work.
Power is a rate, not an amount: the same total energy can be delivered slowly or quickly, and the two are physically different because the time left to react is different.

mysteries.question: How is the energy dissipated by friction partitioned between the two rubbing surfaces?
mysteries.note: The partition depends on temperature, speed and material pair; tribology still models it empirically rather than from first principles.

mysteries.question: Why does time run in one direction rather than both?
mysteries.note: The second law is statistical in the standard account, and the deeper question of why the universe began in a very low-entropy state is not settled by that account.

prompts: A block slides down a rough incline: write the full energy budget and predict where it stops, including the heat produced.
Compare the stopping distance of a car braking from 20 m/s with and without a reaction delay, and explain the difference in energy terms.
Derive the efficiency of a block on a rough incline pushing a load uphill, then check the result against a direct work calculation.

keyNumbers.label: Power of a typical classroom lamp
Energy in one kilogram of fat
Efficiency of a modern electric motor

units.summary: Circular motion is where the vector treatment of force has to be taken seriously: the speed can be constant while the force is anything but, and the word 'centripetal' names a direction rather than a new kind of force.
facts: Uniform circular motion has constant speed but constantly changing velocity, so the acceleration is a = v^2/r directed toward the centre.
'Centripetal force' is simply the name for the net inward force; it is supplied by tension, friction, gravity, magnetism or a normal reaction, not by an extra interaction.
In an inertial frame there is no outward force; the 'centrifugal force' of a rotating frame is a bookkeeping pseudo-force.
Banking a road removes the need for friction: the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force.
For a conical pendulum omega^2 = g/r; for a circular orbit v^2 = GM/r.
The ground itself accelerates: Earth's rotation contributes about 0.034 m/s^2 at the equator, roughly 0.35 % of g, which is why effective g falls with latitude.
In uniform circular motion the acceleration has constant magnitude but a continuously rotating direction, so the velocity vector changes even though its size does not.
conditions: The centripetal analysis assumes a circular path at constant speed; if the speed also changes, a tangential acceleration must be added to the radial one.
The maximum safe speed of a vehicle on a curve is set by the friction limit mu, not by the acceleration itself, and the banking angle shifts that limit.
Working in Earth's rotating frame requires fictitious forces; ignoring them underestimates the effective weight by about 0.35 % at the equator.
Orbital motion neglects drag, tidal perturbation and orbital precession, all of which matter for long-lived satellites.
The centrifugal force is real inside a rotating frame and fictitious in an inertial one; describing a rotating system only works if you say which frame you are using.

mysteries.question: Why do the outer parts of spiral galaxies rotate faster than their visible matter allows?
mysteries.note: The standard explanation is an extended dark-matter halo, but the nature of that halo is unknown and no candidate particle has been confirmed (NASA).

mysteries.question: Why do large, stable polygonal vortices form in rotating fluids, such as the hexagon on Saturn?
mysteries.note: Laboratory experiments reproduce polygonal vortices but do not yet explain the range of sizes and their stability in full.

prompts: Derive the minimum speed at which a car can take a banked curve without depending on friction.
Explain with a free-body diagram why a standing passenger feels pushed outward on a turning bus.
Calculate the change in effective g at the equator caused by Earth's rotation and compare it with the measured value.

keyNumbers.label: Linear speed of the equator from Earth's rotation

sources.label: OpenStax: Uniform and Nonuniform Circular Motion

units.summary: Newton's universal law is the first law of physics that is genuinely universal: the same constant appears for a falling apple and for a galaxy cluster. The unit also contains the sharpest tension between what the law predicts and what we can see.
facts: F = G m1 m2 / r^2 with G = 6.67430e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2, a constant fixed exactly in the 2019 SI and equal and opposite between the two bodies.
g = GM/R^2 = 9.80665 m/s^2 at the surface by definition; the local value varies with latitude and altitude, and in Nepal it is roughly 9.78 to 9.83 m/s^2.
Gravitational potential energy is U = -GMm/r, and the field satisfies g = -grad V, so field and potential are two views of one object.
Escape velocity from the surface is v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) = 11.2 km/s for Earth.
Kepler's three laws follow from the inverse-square law: elliptical orbits with the Sun at a focus, constant areal velocity, and T^2 proportional to a^3.
Galaxy rotation curves and gravitational lensing by clusters both show more gravitating mass than the visible matter accounts for.

The shell theorem makes spherical mass distributions tractable: outside a spherically symmetric body the field is exactly that of a point mass at the centre, which is why planetary orbits have closed-form solutions.
conditions: Newtonian gravity is an excellent approximation for weak fields (GM/rc^2 much less than 1) and slow speeds (v much less than c); near a black-hole horizon and in the early universe it must be replaced by general relativity.
The shell theorem - treating an extended body as a point - needs spherical symmetry, and it fails for flattened or irregular mass distributions such as a disc galaxy or a mountain.
The constant-g treatment near the surface is valid only for heights small compared with Earth's radius; at 3000 m the reduction of g is already about 0.1 %.
Tidal effects, which come from the differential part of the field and scale as r^(-3), govern ocean tides and the Roche limit; the plain 1/r^2 force does not.
Kepler's laws are exact only for two bodies in an inverse-square field; with three or more bodies the orbits are not closed and no exact solution exists.

mysteries.question: What is dark matter made of, and has any candidate particle ever been detected directly?
mysteries.note: No candidate has been confirmed; the evidence is gravitational and the identity is unknown (NASA).

mysteries.question: How did the first stars form, and how long before the first one lit up?
mysteries.note: Dark matter provides the gravitational scaffolding, but the details of the first objects remain an active modelling challenge.

mysteries.question: Can a stable system of planets be configured, and do real systems migrate between configurations?
mysteries.note: Planet-planet scattering, the Lidov-Kozai mechanism and post-Newtonian corrections are all active research areas.

prompts: Compute the escape velocity from the Moon and compare it with the value needed for a crewed mission from Earth.
Measure g in your schoolyard with a simple pendulum, estimate the uncertainty, and compare with the predicted local value.
Derive Kepler's third law from Newton's law of gravitation and check it against the Moon's and Earth's orbital data.

sources.label: OpenStax: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
OpenStax: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion

units.summary: Elasticity turns 'how stiff is this material' into a measurable number with units of pressure, and it separates the regimes in which a material returns to its shape from the regimes in which it does not.
facts: Stress is force per unit area; strain is fractional change in length; Hooke's law says stress is proportional to strain only within the linear elastic regime.
Young's modulus E = stress/strain has the dimensions of pressure and belongs to the material, not to the particular specimen you cut from it.
The stress-strain curve has recognisable regimes: linear elastic, yield, plastic flow, strain hardening, necking and fracture.
Ductile materials give warning before they fail; brittle materials such as glass and cast iron do not, which is why toughness and ductility are engineered separately.
The elastic limit is not the tensile strength: the first marks the end of recoverable deformation, the second the maximum stress the material carries.
The elastic energy stored per unit volume is (1/2) x stress x strain, and Poisson's ratio couples longitudinal strain to lateral contraction.

Stiffness and strength are different properties: the modulus says how much strain a given stress produces, the ultimate stress says how much stress the material survives, and a material can be strong without being stiff.
conditions: Hooke's law needs small strains, an isotropic material, a uniform stress state and a fixed temperature; it fails for rubber (strongly non-Hookean), for plastics beyond the yield point, and for composites loaded off-axis.
Young's modulus depends on temperature and on rate: rubber's modulus rises with strain rate and falls with temperature, which is why a stretched rubber band stiffens when pulled faster.
Fatigue means cyclic loading below the yield strength can still fracture a component after many cycles, and a static tensile test cannot reveal it.
A hole or notch concentrates stress: the local peak stress, not the nominal stress, decides failure, so a small crack can dominate a design.
Poisson's ratio ties lateral strain to longitudinal strain, so no solid can be perfectly incompressible and perfectly isotropic at once; most engineering metals sit near 0.3.

mysteries.question: Can the strength of a material be predicted from its atomic structure alone?
mysteries.note: Dislocation theory explains strength qualitatively; quantitative prediction for real materials remains a research problem.

mysteries.question: How do microscopic defects nucleate and grow into the cracks that end a component's life?
mysteries.note: The mechanisms are known in outline, and fatigue-life prediction for specific parts remains an engineering challenge.

prompts: Plot a stress-strain curve for a steel wire or a plastic strip and label every regime you can identify.
Design an experiment to find Young's modulus of a bamboo strip, and state the dominant uncertainty in your result.
Explain, with an example, why a sharp crack is more dangerous than a round hole of the same size.

keyNumbers.label: Young's modulus of bone (along the shaft)
Ultimate tensile strength of mild steel

sources.label: OpenStax: Stress, Strain and Elastic Modulus

units.summary: The distinction between heat and temperature is the doorway to thermodynamics. Heat is energy in transit, temperature is a property of a body, and the zeroth law is what makes thermometers possible at all.
facts: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; it is a process quantity, not a substance stored inside an object.
Temperature measures the average microscopic kinetic energy of particles, with the equipartition theorem distributing energy across the available degrees of freedom.
The zeroth law - if A equals B thermally and B equals C, then A equals C - is what makes a thermometer a thermometer.
Temperature is intensive; heat and internal energy are extensive, so they scale with the amount of matter.
The kelvin is defined by the Boltzmann constant, k = 1.380649e-23 J/K exactly, and is the only SI scale proportional to a true zero.
Thermal equilibrium is dynamic: microscopic energy exchange continues forever, but with no net flow in either direction.
Temperature is a state variable made meaningful by the zeroth law, while heat is a path-dependent transfer; the two are different kinds of quantity and are not interchangeable inside an equation.
conditions: 'Temperature equals average kinetic energy' is exact for a monatomic ideal gas; for molecules with rotation and vibration the equipartition theorem spreads the energy over more degrees of freedom.
A thermometer reading is the equilibrium temperature of the thermometer-object pair, so the reading lags and can measurably disturb a small object.
At nanometre and smaller scales, different definitions of temperature (electronic, vibrational, configurational) need not agree, so 'the temperature' of a nanoscale system can be ambiguous.
Temperature scales other than kelvin are proportional only over a limited range; Celsius and Fahrenheit diverge as you approach absolute zero.
Thermodynamic equilibrium requires thermal and mechanical balance together, so a sealed system can be at thermal equilibrium and still be pushing on its surroundings.

mysteries.question: Can two bodies at the same temperature still exchange heat?
mysteries.note: Yes - equilibrium is statistical and exchange continues in both directions, but the net flow vanishes; the statistical statement is what makes the zeroth law a law.

mysteries.question: Is there a single, unique temperature for a system far from equilibrium?
mysteries.note: Different definitions diverge for non-equilibrium and nanoscale systems, and no universal choice is settled.

prompts: Rewrite the sentence 'the bucket of water has a lot of heat in it' so that it is physically correct, and explain what is wrong with the original.
Explain why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon at the same room temperature.
Derive the final temperature of two bodies placed in thermal contact from conservation of energy and a constant-heat-capacity model.

units.summary: Most solids expand when heated and water does something stranger. The coefficient of expansion is a property with a pedigree - it tracks bond strength - and it is the hidden variable in precision engineering, from railway gaps to cryogenic mirrors.
facts: For modest temperature changes dL = alpha L dT; alpha is the linear coefficient of expansion and depends on material, temperature and direction.
Expansion coefficients are broadly inversely related to bond strength, so stiff, high-melting-point materials such as fused silica expand far less than rubber or lead.
Water is anomalous: it contracts on cooling from 100 degrees C to 4 degrees C and expands on freezing, which is why lakes freeze from the top down and pipes burst in winter.
A bimetallic strip converts a temperature change into mechanical motion - the working principle of every household thermostat.
The Gruneisen parameter links expansion to compressibility and heat capacity through alpha V K_s = gamma C_V.
Gaps in rails, joints in bridges and expansion joints in concrete are all the same idea: the material will change size, so the structure must allow it.

Thermal expansion comes from anharmonicity in the interatomic potential: the average separation between neighbours grows with temperature, and the expansion coefficient is that average increase per kelvin.
conditions: The linear law is a first-order approximation; it fails for large temperature changes, near phase transitions and for anisotropic materials such as graphite or wood.
For an isotropic solid the volume coefficient is approximately three times the linear coefficient, and the equality holds only in the small-expansion limit.
Apparent expansion of a liquid must subtract the container's own expansion, which for mercury in glass can be about 2 % of the reading.
As temperature approaches absolute zero the expansion coefficient vanishes, which is why cryogenic instruments use alloys such as Invar and Kovar whose expansion is nearly zero.

The linear expansion law is a first-order approximation for small temperature changes; a body cooling towards absolute zero needs the integrated form, because the coefficient itself varies with temperature.

mysteries.question: Can thermal expansion be harnessed directly to produce useful electrical power?
mysteries.note: Thermal diodes, phase-change engines and flexoelectric effects are active research areas, but the efficiencies remain far below those of conventional heat engines.

mysteries.question: Why does water expand when it freezes, when almost every other substance contracts?
mysteries.note: Hydrogen bonds give ice an open lattice; the same anomaly is what lets a lake freeze from the top down.

prompts: Design a bimetallic strip switch and calculate the tip displacement for a given temperature change.
Explain why a mercury thermometer left in a freezer shows a rise in reading rather than a fall.
Compare the thermal design of the JWST's cryogenic mirror segments with a classroom thermometer and state the common principle.

keyNumbers.label: Volume expansion of water near 20 degrees C

units.summary: Quantity of heat is where the first law becomes arithmetic: energy accounting with a heat capacity, a latent heat and a clear statement of which system you are describing.
facts: Q = m c dT requires no phase change, a constant specific heat over the range, and a clearly defined system.
Specific heat capacity is per unit mass; the molar heat capacity is C = M c, where M is the molar mass.
During a phase change the temperature stays constant while heat is added, because the energy goes into changing the structure rather than the motion of the particles.
Latent heat enters as Q = m L; the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water at 100 degrees C is about 2.26e6 J/kg.
Internal energy is a state function of the body; heat is the transfer, and the first law writes dQ = dU + dW with work done by the system positive.
Calorimetry rests on the statement that heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold one - true only for an isolated system.

Heat capacity is quoted along constant volume or constant pressure because only the path-independent change of internal energy is the same for both; the difference between them is the work done by expansion.
conditions: The constant-c approximation fails for gases, whose heat capacity varies with temperature, and for any interval that crosses a phase change.
Latent heat is not a universal constant: it varies with pressure and temperature, and for water it falls as the critical point is approached.
Calorimetry assumes an isolated system; in a real cup the heat capacity of the container must be included, and it often dominates the error.
Specific heat of water is commonly approximated as 4.18 kJ/(kg.K) over 0 to 100 degrees C, but it varies by more than 1 % across that range.
Water's large specific heat is a symptom of hydrogen-bonded network rearrangements, not a separate slow-to-heat mechanism, and it is the reason oceans moderate coastal climate.

mysteries.question: How is energy distributed among the translational, rotational and vibrational modes of a molecule as its temperature rises?
mysteries.note: Equipartition gives the high-temperature limit and quantum theory gives the low-temperature limit; the crossover in real materials is modelled, not derived.

mysteries.question: Can the heat capacity of a complex solid be computed from first principles to experimental accuracy?
mysteries.note: Modern ab initio methods approximate it well for simple crystals; no exact general theory exists.

prompts: Plan a calorimetry experiment to determine the specific heat of a metal and list every systematic error you can foresee.
Show quantitatively why 1 kg of steam at 100 degrees C can release more energy than 1 kg of water at 100 degrees C.
Estimate the energy needed to heat a classroom by 10 degrees C and compare it with a student's daily food intake.

keyNumbers.label: Latent heat of vaporisation of water (100 degrees C)
Specific latent heat of fusion of water at 0 degrees C
Energy to raise 1 kg of water by 1 K

sources.label: OpenStax: Heat Transfer, Specific Heat and Calorimetry

units.summary: How fast energy moves as heat depends on the mechanism: contact, bulk motion of a fluid, or electromagnetic radiation. Each mechanism has its own law, its own geometry, and its own place where the textbook approximation fails.
facts: Conduction transfers energy through a medium without moving the medium; convection moves bulk fluid; radiation needs no medium at all.
Fourier's law states dQ/dt = -k A dT/dx, with thermal conductivity k a material property and the minus sign meaning heat flows down the temperature gradient.
Newton's law of cooling gives the convective rate dQ/dt = h A (T_surface - T_fluid), with h the convection coefficient, which depends on flow conditions rather than on geometry alone.
The Stefan-Boltzmann law for a blackbody is P = epsilon sigma A T^4, with sigma = 5.670374419e-8 W/(m^2.K^4) exactly in the 2019 SI.
Thermal resistances add in series and parallel exactly like electrical resistances, with R = L/(kA) for a slab.
Building heat loss, the thermal performance of a wall, and the ability of a device to shed heat are all set by this network of resistances.

Conduction, convection and radiation are three separate mechanisms: conduction is the diffusion of particle energy through a medium, convection needs a moving fluid, and radiation needs no medium at all.
conditions: Fourier's law in its simple slab form assumes steady or quasi-steady state with a one-dimensional gradient; fast transients with a sharp thermal front need the heat equation instead.
At nanometre gaps, interfacial (Kapitza) resistance dominates, so the bulk conductivity alone badly under-predicts the thermal resistance of a nanostructure.
Radiation dominates above a few hundred degrees Celsius and in vacuum, so insulation design that ignores it fails in exactly the conditions where it matters most.
The Stefan-Boltzmann law as written is for a blackbody; real surfaces need an emissivity, and a non-grey surface needs a spectral integral rather than a single epsilon.
Newton's law of cooling assumes convective loss to air near ambient temperature; at high temperature radiative loss dominates and the cooling curve changes shape.

mysteries.question: How is heat carried across a single atomic layer - by phonons, by electrons, or by something else?
mysteries.note: Ballistic, diffusive and hydrodynamic transport regimes have all been observed in graphene and other two-dimensional materials, and the boundaries between them are still being mapped.

mysteries.question: How much cooling power will future quantum processors demand, and what will set the limit?
mysteries.note: Cooling power rises steeply below about 20 K, and the practical limits of cryogenic infrastructure are an active engineering constraint.

prompts: Calculate the heat loss through a wall, then repeat for a double-glazed design, and set out the thermal resistance network explicitly.
Explain why a metal spoon and a wooden spoon feel different although both conduct heat.
Design a method for measuring the emissivity of a dark surface using a lamp and a thermometer, and estimate its uncertainty.

keyNumbers.label: Thermal resistance of 20 cm of brick (k = 0.7 W/(m.K))

units.summary: The ideal gas is a model with a stated domain: it works when molecules are far apart and barely interacting. Its real value is that it links temperature to microscopic motion, so the same equation can be read as a statement about atoms.
facts: PV = nRT with R = 8.314462618 J/(mol.K) exactly in the 2019 SI, where n is the amount of substance in moles.
Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws are limiting cases of the ideal-gas equation, valid at low density and at temperatures well above condensation.
Kinetic theory gives P = (1/3)(N/V) m <v^2>, so the pressure of a gas is the momentum transfer from its molecules hitting the walls.
For a monatomic gas the mean translational kinetic energy is (3/2) k T, and the rms speed is sqrt(3RT/M).
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, U = n C_V T, and for a monatomic gas C_V = 3R/2.
Mayer's relation C_P - C_V = R follows from the first law together with the ideal-gas equation.
The ideal gas law is a limit rather than a definition: it holds exactly only at infinite dilution, and real gases show the condensation and critical behaviour the law cannot describe.
conditions: The model needs negligible molecular volume and negligible intermolecular forces: low density and a temperature well above the condensation temperature.
The van der Waals equation (P + a n^2/V^2)(V - nb) = nRT corrects the two main failures - attractive forces (a) and finite molecular size (b).
Equipartition, and therefore the plateau value of the heat capacity, fails at low temperature where the quantum energy levels are not thermally populated.
A gas in equilibrium has a single pressure and temperature; a non-equilibrium gas has neither, so the equation of state cannot even be written down.
Kinetic theory needs equipartition, which fails once the quantum level spacing is comparable to kT - exactly why helium must be cooled below about 4 K to liquefy.

mysteries.question: Can translational motion be cooled below the quantum ground state of the confining potential?
mysteries.note: Laser and evaporative cooling reach picokelvin temperatures for motion, but a confinement potential has a lowest level that cannot be crossed; how that floor depends on the geometry is still open.

mysteries.question: Why does the heat capacity of a gas rise in steps at low temperature while a solid's varies smoothly?
mysteries.note: Rotational and vibrational levels freeze out one by one below their characteristic temperatures - the Debye, rotor and oscillator models - which is settled for idealised cases and still refined for real materials.

prompts: Compute the rms speed of nitrogen molecules at room temperature and compare it with the speed of sound in air.
Use the first law and C_V to show that the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature.
Plot the P-V diagrams of an ideal gas and a van der Waals gas and mark the region where real behaviour departs.

keyNumbers.label: Standard molar volume at 0 degrees C, 1 atm
Boiling point of liquid nitrogen at 1 atm

sources.label: OpenStax: Molecular Model of an Ideal Gas
OpenStax: Heat Capacity and Equipartition of Energy

units.summary: Curved mirrors turn the law of reflection into an imaging device. Everything in the unit rests on one approximation - rays close to the principal axis - and on one convention that, used inconsistently, produces most of the wrong answers.
facts: The focal length of a spherical mirror is half the radius of curvature, f = R/2; concave mirrors converge and convex mirrors diverge.
A convex mirror always produces a virtual, upright and diminished image of a real object, which is why it is the safe choice for a vehicle mirror.
The mirror equation 1/f = 1/v + 1/u and the magnification m = -v/u hold under the New Cartesian sign convention.

Three principal rays suffice for any ray diagram: parallel to the axis (reflected through the focus), through the centre of curvature (reflected back on itself), and through the focus (reflected parallel to the axis).
The point focus of a spherical mirror exists only in the paraxial approximation; spherical aberration grows rapidly with the aperture.
The 18 hexagonal segments of the JWST mirror are aligned to act as a single 6.5 m primary, focused to a precision of a small fraction of the width of a human hair.
A spherical mirror has a single focus only while the aperture is small compared with the radius of curvature; beyond that, spherical aberration spreads the focus and the image softens with age.
conditions: Mirror and lens formulae are paraxial: the rays must be close to the principal axis. Wide apertures require real ray tracing or an aspherical surface such as a parabola.
A real image can be caught on a screen; a virtual image cannot be projected, which is the physical difference behind the two categories.
Mixing sign conventions is the single most common source of wrong signs; fix one convention and use it in every diagram.
For a mirror moving at speed, the image can appear to move faster than light; no information travels faster than light because the image is an optical construction, not a material object.
The mirror equation and magnification are paraxial results; a wide field of view needs aberration-corrected designs such as the Ritchey-Chretien and active mirrors like JWST's.

mysteries.question: Can an optical system form a perfect image of an extended object across a wide field of view?
mysteries.note: Aberration theory rules out perfect imaging with simple surfaces; multi-element and wave-optics designs trade cost against the remaining errors, and no system is perfect.

mysteries.question: How far can real-time adaptive optics push atmospheric correction for ground-based telescopes?
mysteries.note: Correction works extremely well for well-resolved guide stars, and the limit is set by sensor speed, guide-star availability and photon flux.

prompts: Construct ray diagrams for an object at infinity, beyond C, at C, between C and F, and at F for a concave mirror, and tabulate image position, nature and magnification.
Explain why a vehicle's wing mirror is convex rather than flat, and why the image of a following car looks smaller than it is.
A concave mirror has f = 20 cm and the object is 30 cm in front of it: find the image position and magnification, and decide whether the image is real.

keyNumbers.label: JWST mirror alignment tolerance
keyNumbers.value: about 1/10000 of a human hair's width

keyNumbers.label: Focal length of a concave mirror of radius 20 cm

units.summary: Refraction at a plane boundary is Snell's law, but the interesting physics is in the consequences: the lateral shift through a slab, the shallower apparent depth of a pool, and total internal reflection, which is the whole basis of fibre optics.
facts: Snell's law reads n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2), with n = c/v the refractive index; the frequency of light is unchanged at the boundary while its speed and wavelength change.
A plane-parallel slab displaces the emergent ray sideways while keeping it parallel to the incident ray; the displacement grows with thickness and with obliquity.
Total internal reflection requires n1 > n2 and an incidence angle above the critical angle theta_c = arcsin(n2/n1), about 41.1 degrees for crown glass (n = 1.52) against air.
Viewed near-normally, an object in water appears shallower by a factor of about n, so a 1.5 m depth reads as about 1.1 m.
Optical fibres work by repeated total internal reflection; the acceptance angle is fixed by the numerical aperture of the core and cladding.
In the wave picture refraction follows from phase continuity at the boundary: the phase must match across it, which is Snell's law in a different costume.
Snell's law is a statement about phase continuity across a boundary: the change of direction is what keeps the wavefronts in step, and the same law governs light as a wave and as a quantum field.
conditions: Snell's law assumes an isotropic, homogeneous, stationary, non-absorbing medium and a smooth interface; rough or moving boundaries change the result.
Near the critical angle the transmitted ray grazes the surface and the reflection coefficient approaches one.
The simple apparent-depth rule (divide by n) holds only for near-normal viewing; at oblique angles the correct factor is cos(theta')/cos(theta).
Dispersion - the wavelength dependence of n - is neglected in the basic model but must be included whenever white light is involved.
Fermat's principle fixes the path of least time rather than least distance, and that distinction is why a refracted ray bends towards the normal in a denser medium.

mysteries.question: Can an image be formed that is not limited by the diffraction limit?
mysteries.note: Superlenses using negative-index materials beat the diffraction limit at a single frequency; extending the idea to a usable bandwidth remains an open and difficult problem.

mysteries.question: Why does light slow down in a medium without losing energy?
mysteries.note: The classical account through the material's dielectric response is standard, while the fully microscopic picture of coherent forward scattering is subtler.

prompts: Compute the lateral shift of a ray through a glass slab and verify the prediction with a pencil, a glass block and a sheet of paper.
Design an optical fibre for a given numerical aperture and explain the role of the cladding.
Explain why a swimming pool looks shallower at the far end, and derive the apparent depth for oblique viewing.

keyNumbers.label: Critical angle, crown glass to air
Critical angle for water to air

units.summary: A prism is a device that separates wavelengths as it bends them. The unit connects geometry to spectroscopy: the apex angle sets the deviation, the refractive index sets the dispersion, and the spectrum is the primary chemical and astronomical fingerprint of light.
facts: A prism deviates light because its faces are not parallel, and it disperses light because the refractive index depends on wavelength - normally n is larger for blue than for red.
For a thin prism of small apex angle A, the deviation is approximately d = (n - 1) A.
The dispersive power w = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1) is nearly constant for a given material, which is why glasses can be sorted into crown and flint families.
Minimum deviation occurs when the ray path is symmetric (i = e), giving n = sin((A + d_m)/2) / sin(A/2) - the standard laboratory method.
A hollow prism filled with a liquid measures that liquid's refractive index by the same minimum-deviation method.
The rainbow is refraction plus one internal reflection plus dispersion in water droplets, which is why the primary bow has an angle of about 42 degrees.

At minimum deviation the ray path is symmetric, so the refractive index can be measured without knowing the prism's apex angle precisely - which is why the spectrometer method is the reference technique.
conditions: The thin-prism approximation requires a small apex angle; thick prisms need the exact two-surface treatment with Snell's law applied twice.
Dispersion is small - the index changes by only about 0.01 to 0.02 across the visible for glass - so a single prism gives a spectrum whose orders overlap and may need a second prism to isolate.
Deviation depends on the refractive index of the surrounding medium: a prism in water disperses far less than the same prism in air.
Refractive index depends on temperature as well as wavelength, so precision spectroscopy requires controlling the temperature of the prism.
The small-angle formula n = 1 + A/2D is an approximation that fails beyond about 10 degrees of deviation; real work uses the exact minimum-deviation relation.

mysteries.question: How do modern observatories push spectroscopy to fainter objects than the classical prism or grating allowed?
mysteries.note: Very large telescopes, échelle spectrographs and interferometry have extended the reach, and each gain is limited by photon collection and detector noise.

mysteries.question: Can a dispersive element be built that disperses without deviating, or deviates without dispersing?
mysteries.note: Compound and metamaterial designs approach these limits, but causality constrains how well an achromatic, deviation-free element can behave over a finite bandwidth.

prompts: Given the deviation angles of red and violet light through a 60 degree prism, find the two refractive indices and hence the dispersive power.
Measure the angle of minimum deviation for a triangular glass prism, compute n, and repeat with a hollow prism filled with water.
Explain geometrically why the deviation of a prism does not grow in proportion to the thickness of the glass.

units.summary: Lenses bend light to make images, and the thin-lens equation is the workhorse of the entire unit. What separates school physics from optical engineering is the list of assumptions that equation hides: thinness, paraxial rays, and a single refractive index.
facts: The thin-lens equation is 1/f = 1/v - 1/u under the usual sign convention, and the lensmaker's equation gives 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2) for a lens in air.
The power of a lens is P = 1/f in dioptres; for a lens immersed in a medium of index n_m it becomes (n_l/n_m - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2).
A converging lens is thicker at the centre and a diverging lens is thinner at the centre; for a real object a diverging lens always gives a virtual, upright, diminished image.
In contact, P = P1 + P2; separated by a distance d, the equivalent power is 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2 - d/(f1 f2).
The human eye is a roughly 17 mm lens with a focal length of about 2.3 cm; accommodation works by changing the lens curvature so the image always lands on the retina.
Magnification m = v/u, and a real image is inverted and can be projected on a screen.

A lens forms a real or virtual image depending on where the object sits relative to the focal length, and the thin-lens treatment hides the thick-lens corrections and aberrations that real objectives need.
conditions: The thin-lens equation requires a lens thin compared with its focal length and paraxial rays; real camera and telescope lenses are thick assemblies whose elements cancel aberrations.
Chromatic aberration means f depends on wavelength, so a single glass lens focuses blue and red at different distances; an achromatic doublet combines glasses of different dispersion to cancel it.
Spherical aberration grows with aperture, so stopping down a camera trades brightness for sharpness - until diffraction takes over.
Depth of field depends on aperture and focal length as well as on the sensor, so it is a property of the optical system, not of the camera body.
The lensmaker's equation assumes a thin lens in air; a thick or multi-element system is described by its principal planes and effective focal length instead.

mysteries.question: How do observatories image exoplanets that are thousands of light-years away and a few pixels across?
mysteries.note: Coronagraphs, adaptive optics and interferometry are combined to suppress starlight by many orders of magnitude, and each step adds its own noise.

mysteries.question: Is there a fundamental limit to how small an optical element can be before diffraction dominates?
mysteries.note: Abbe's limit sets the classical bound and super-resolution can cross it only in restricted ways; how far this can be pushed for imaging remains an active question.

prompts: Two thin lenses of focal length 10 cm and 15 cm are placed 5 cm apart: find the equivalent focal length and locate the image of an object 30 cm from the first lens.
Design an achromatic doublet from two glass types and explain the trade-off between focal length, spherical aberration and cost.
Explain why closing the aperture improves depth of field but introduces diffraction blur, and find the aperture that balances the two.

keyNumbers.label: Focal length of the human eye
Airy disk angular radius at 550 nm (D = 0.1 m)
Refractive index of the human cornea
Near point of a normal eye

units.summary: Dispersion is the wavelength dependence of refractive index. It explains rainbows and chromatic aberration, it is the reason a spectrum carries chemical information, and it contains one of the sharpest traps in optics: the difference between phase velocity and the speed that carries information.
facts: Dispersion means n depends on wavelength, so different colours bend by different amounts and a lens focuses them at different distances.
Cauchy's empirical form n = A + B/lambda^2 gives an approximate wavelength dependence in transparent regions.
Normal dispersion - n rising as lambda falls - is what produces the familiar spectrum order from red to violet.
Anomalous dispersion near an absorption band reverses the sign of dn/dlambda, and a dispersive prism can then select a single narrow band from white light.
The group velocity v_g = c/(n - lambda dn/dlambda) can exceed c or become negative in anomalously dispersive media without violating relativity, because the phase velocity carries no information.
A spectrum is a fingerprint: the blackbody shape gives temperature, the line positions give composition, and the Doppler shift gives motion.
Glass has a larger refractive index for blue light than for red, so short wavelengths are bent more and a prism sends violet towards the inside of the spectrum.
conditions: Cauchy's two-parameter fit is valid only for normal dispersion in transparent regions; it diverges near a resonance and cannot describe absorption at all.
Information travels at the group velocity, so superluminal phase velocity is a feature of the mathematics, not a violation of causality.
At a boundary between media the frequency of light does not change; what changes is the speed and hence the wavelength - a classic examination trap.
Spectral lines are broadened by temperature, pressure and Doppler motion, and that broadening sets the precision with which a line centre can be measured.
In a dispersive medium the group velocity differs from the phase velocity, so the speed of light in glass quoted as c/n is a phase speed and not the speed at which a pulse front travels.

mysteries.question: Can a dispersion profile be engineered that resolves wavelengths beyond the diffraction limit of the device itself?
mysteries.note: Metasurface and metamaterial designs are actively pursuing this; causality and usable bandwidth are the limiting constraints.

mysteries.question: How are atomic energy levels and their linewidths set, and how far can they be predicted from first principles?
mysteries.note: Spectroscopy is precise enough to test atomic theory at parts per billion, which keeps refining rather than contradicting it.

prompts: Using Cauchy's formula and a measured index at two wavelengths, predict the order in which colours emerge from a prism.
Explain why the same prism shows a much narrower spectrum when immersed in water.
Compare the resolving power of a prism and a diffraction grating for the same beam width, and identify which is better for faint astronomical sources.

keyNumbers.label: Speed of light in crown glass (n = 1.52)
Angular dispersion of a 60 degree crown-glass prism

units.summary: Electric charge is the first conserved quantity a student meets that is exactly conserved in every known interaction. The unit also contains one of the cleanest pieces of evidence in all of physics: charge is quantised, and the quantum is exact.
facts: Charge is quantised: the elementary charge e = 1.602176634e-19 C exactly, and every observed charge in ordinary matter is an integer multiple of it.
Coulomb's law F = k q1 q2 / r^2 holds with k = 8.9875517923e9 N.m^2/C^2, and like charges repel while unlike charges attract.
Charge is conserved in every known interaction, and electric charge is an exact conserved quantum number in the Standard Model.
Charging by friction transfers electrons between surfaces; charging by induction moves electrons without any contact at all.
Conductors allow charge to move freely and insulators do not; in electrostatic equilibrium the field inside a conductor is zero and excess charge sits on the surface, concentrating at sharp points.
Earthing works because the Earth is an enormous conductor held at nearly constant potential.

Charge is quantised in units of e; the fractional charges seen in the fractional quantum Hall effect are a many-body property of a correlated electron liquid, not evidence that the electron is divisible.
conditions: Coulomb's law assumes static point charges in a uniform medium; extended bodies require integration and conductors require redistribution.
Charging by friction depends on the material pair, surface condition and humidity - the triboelectric order is a tendency, not a law.
The field inside a conductor is zero only in electrostatic equilibrium; a time-varying field drives currents inside it.
In semiconductors both electrons and holes carry current, so 'the charge carrier' model of a conductor has to be replaced by a two-carrier picture.
Coulomb's law is the static, vacuum result; for moving charges the magnetic field joins in, and an accelerating charge radiates, so the static formula alone no longer describes the system.

mysteries.question: Why is electric charge quantised, and can fractional charge ever be observed?
mysteries.note: The Standard Model contains charge quantisation but does not derive it; quasiparticles with fractional charge do exist in certain condensed-matter states, which is a different phenomenon.

mysteries.question: Is electric charge exactly conserved?
mysteries.note: Experiments constrain any violation to an extraordinarily small level; neutron-decay searches continue to sharpen that bound.

prompts: Explain why a charged rod attracts a neutral paper strip, and draw the induced polarisation on the strip.
Predict the charge distribution on a hollow conducting sphere and on a sphere containing an off-centre cavity.
Compute how many electrons correspond to a charge of 1 nC and comment on what that says about the quantisation of charge.

keyNumbers.label: Force between two protons 1 m apart

units.summary: The electric field turns a force law into a description of the space around a charge: it says what force a test charge would feel at every point, whether or not one is actually there.
facts: The electric field is force per unit positive test charge, E = F/q, directed along the force on a positive test charge.
A point charge produces E = kq/r^2 directed radially, and superposition means the total field is the vector sum of the individual fields.
Field lines are a visualisation, not a count of anything: their density represents field strength, they start on positive charge and end on negative charge, and they never cross.
The field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero; the field of an infinite non-conducting sheet is sigma/(2 epsilon0), and of a conducting sheet sigma/epsilon0.
Because F = qE for any charge, the field can be treated as an independent variable - the reason Gauss's law is so powerful.
A moving charge creates a magnetic field as well, so the electric and magnetic fields of a charge are two aspects of a single electromagnetic field.
Field lines are bookkeeping: the number crossing a surface is proportional to the flux, so a denser bundle means a stronger field, even though the lines themselves have no physical substance.
conditions: Closed-form field results exist only where symmetry is high enough - spherical, cylindrical or planar; any other distribution requires integration.
Electrostatic fields are conservative, so the work around a closed path vanishes and a scalar potential can be used instead.
In a dielectric the field is reduced by the relative permittivity, and polarisation P must be introduced; writing E = F/q with a 'free' charge only is wrong inside matter.
Electrostatic reasoning does not extend to time-varying fields: Maxwell's displacement current means a changing electric field generates a magnetic field.
Superposition is a statement about linear response, and real dielectrics are generally not linear, so polarisation and non-linear media need their own treatment.

mysteries.question: How does a charge act on matter that is not charged?
mysteries.note: The field picture handles it through polarisation; whether the field itself is physical or a bookkeeping device is a deeper interpretational question.

mysteries.question: Can a static field be completely screened in any geometry?
mysteries.note: Only conductors screen, and the shape of the screening conductor matters; a fully screened, shape-independent result is not generally available.

prompts: Find the field on the axis of a uniformly charged ring and show where it reaches its maximum.
Show that two infinite sheets carrying opposite uniform charges produce a uniform field between them and zero outside.
Plot the field of an electric dipole along its axis and compare with the far-field 1/r^3 law.

keyNumbers.label: Field at 1 nm from a proton
Field at the surface of a proton (radius 0.84 fm)
Fair-weather field at the Earth's surface

units.summary: Potential is the scalar alternative to the vector field. Because only differences are measurable, the zero of potential is a convention - and because the field is conservative, path never enters the answer.
facts: Electric potential is energy per unit charge, V = U/q, and a potential difference is the work done per unit charge by the field.
For a point charge V = kq/r with V tending to zero at infinity, and the potential difference is dV = -E.dl along any path.
Only potential differences are physically meaningful; the choice of zero is a convention, and it changes no experiment.
The potential energy of a system of point charges is the sum of pairwise terms q1 q2/(4 pi epsilon0 r_ij); the self-energy of a continuous distribution requires a self-consistent calculation.
Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines, and the work in moving a charge between two points on the same equipotential is zero.
Potential is a scalar, which is why circuit and field problems are often shorter in potential language than in field language.
Potential is defined only up to an additive constant, so only differences are physical; a conductor is one equipotential surface, and the field is minus the gradient of the potential.
conditions: The 1/r potential law assumes a point charge in vacuum; for a conductor the entire surface is one equipotential at a single value.
Potential differences are path-independent, so only the endpoints matter - but a potential difference between two points is not simply E.d unless the path is straight and along the field.
Moving a charge changes the stored energy of the whole system, and the work is shared between the field and the agent that moves it.
In a medium with permittivity epsilon the potential of a charge is reduced by the factor epsilon_r; the free charge does not change, the field does.
The expression U = qV holds for a conservative, time-independent field; in a time-varying field the work done on the charge also changes the energy stored in the field itself.

mysteries.question: How much energy is stored in an electromagnetic field, and how is it distributed in space?
mysteries.note: Classically the energy density is (1/2) epsilon E^2 plus a magnetic term; the quantum description in terms of photons remains less intuitive.

mysteries.question: Can energy be extracted usefully from the vacuum?
mysteries.note: Casimir and related effects are real and measurable but tiny; extracting macroscopic energy from vacuum fluctuations is not established.

prompts: Compute the potential on the axis of a uniformly charged disc and identify its far-field limit.
Show in one dimension that E = -dV/dx, using a finite-difference argument rather than calculus.
Compare the energy stored in a charged capacitor with the work required to charge it, and explain why they are equal.

keyNumbers.label: Field between the plates of a charged parallel-plate capacitor
Potential of the Earth's surface relative to infinity
Energy gained by an electron accelerated through 100 V

sources.label: OpenStax: Electric Potential and Potential Difference

units.summary: A capacitor is an energy store defined by geometry and dielectric. The unit is where the parallel-plate formula gets derived from Gauss's law, and where students first meet the gap between an ideal component and a real one.
facts: Capacitance is C = Q/V; for a parallel-plate capacitor C = epsilon0 epsilon_r A/d, so capacitance grows with area and shrinks with separation.
The energy stored is U = (1/2) C V^2 = Q^2/(2C), and the energy density in the dielectric is u = (1/2) epsilon E^2.
Capacitors in parallel add capacitance; in series the reciprocals add.
A capacitor stores energy rather than supplying it: an ideal charged capacitor discharges through any available path, and the discharge time constant is R C.
Real capacitors are limited by dielectric breakdown, leakage current, equivalent series resistance and self-inductance at high frequency.
Supercapacitors deliver far more power than batteries but store far less energy per kilogram, and the two technologies occupy different niches for that reason.

Capacitance depends on geometry and dielectric only, never on the charge or the voltage: adding dielectric raises the capacitance by the permittivity ratio, and a connected battery supplies the extra charge at unchanged voltage.
conditions: The parallel-plate formula assumes the separation is much smaller than the plate dimensions, so fringing can be ignored, and that the dielectric fills the gap uniformly.
In a dielectric the bound charges reduce the field by 1/epsilon_r, but the energy per unit volume usually still increases because polarisation contributes.
At DC, leakage limits how long a charge can be held; at high frequency, inductance and ESR dominate, and the ideal capacitor stops being a capacitor.
Electrolytic capacitors are polar and will be destroyed by reverse voltage, while ceramic and film types are non-polar but have different leakage and stability behaviour.
The stored energy lives in the electric field, not in the charges; discharging a capacitor does not lose that energy, it converts it back into current and heat.

mysteries.question: How can more energy be stored at a higher voltage in a smaller volume?
mysteries.note: Solid electrolytes, nanostructured dielectrics and breakdown engineering are all being pursued, and each trades cost, reliability and lifetime against energy density.

mysteries.question: Is there a fundamental upper bound to the energy that can be stored in a given volume?
mysteries.note: Fundamental limits exist, including the scale at which the vacuum itself breaks down, but they lie far above present engineering practice.

prompts: Derive the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor from Gauss's law and the definition C = Q/V.
Compare the stored energy of a 1 F supercapacitor at 2.7 V with that of a 2000 mAh lithium-ion cell at 3.7 V, and compare their power delivery.
Design a smoothing network for a rectified supply and justify the ripple calculation with the RC time constant.

keyNumbers.label: Energy in a 2000 mAh cell at 3.7 V
Energy stored in a 1 F supercapacitor at 2.7 V

sources.label: OpenStax: Energy Stored in a Capacitor

units.summary: Circuit analysis is conservation law with a convenient vocabulary: charge conservation becomes Kirchhoff's current law, energy conservation becomes the loop law, and Ohm's law is the constitutive relation that connects them - where it is allowed to apply.
facts: Ohm's law V = IR describes ohmic components only; a filament lamp and a diode are non-ohmic, with resistance that changes as current or temperature changes.
Kirchhoff's current law is charge conservation at a node; the loop law is energy conservation around a closed path.
Series resistances add and parallel conductances add, so series-parallel reduction is the workhorse method for solvable networks.
A source with internal resistance r delivers V = E - Ir, so its terminal voltage falls as the current it supplies rises.
Maximum power transfer to the load occurs when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, but then only half of the generated power reaches the load.
Joule heating P = I^2 R is why conductors and components get hot, and rated wattage is what limits safe operation.
Kirchhoff's laws are bookkeeping identities - charge conservation and energy conservation in disguise - so they hold for any lumped circuit regardless of the physics of the individual elements.
conditions: The lumped-circuit model assumes ideal wires and components that are small compared with the wavelength; at high frequencies transmission lines and distributed effects take over.
Kirchhoff's laws assume quasi-static behaviour, so no charge accumulates inside the wires and each node has a well-defined potential.
Ohmic behaviour is temperature-dependent, so treating R as constant is an approximation that matters in power calculations.
A real battery is not a fixed source: its terminal voltage and internal resistance both depend on state of charge, temperature and current.
Series and parallel reduction assumes ideal wires and lumped elements; at high frequency the wire's own resistance and inductance take over and the ideal rules stop holding.

mysteries.question: What sets the energy floor for computing with superconducting circuits?
mysteries.note: Superconducting qubits and single-photon detectors push towards the energy-time uncertainty limit for readout, which is now the binding constraint in several architectures.

mysteries.question: Can computation be performed with less energy per operation than a transistor switch requires?
mysteries.note: Landauer sets a thermodynamic floor and the end of Moore's-law scaling has moved the constraint into interconnect and memory energy.

units.summary: Nuclear physics is where conservation laws become non-negotiable and where a handful of nucleons produce an enormous energy scale. The binding-energy curve is the centre of the unit: it explains why fusion and fission both release energy, and only in different regimes.
facts: The nuclear radius scales as R = R0 A^(1/3) with R0 about 1.2 fm, which means nuclear density is roughly constant at about 2.3e17 kg/m^3.
Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV per nucleon, so fusion up to iron and fission beyond it both release energy.
Einstein's E = mc^2 converts the mass defect into binding energy; 1 u of mass corresponds to 931.5 MeV.
Radioactive decay is statistical: the half-life is a property of the nucleus, and no individual atom decides when it decays.
Neutron decay and nuclear reactions conserve charge, baryon number, energy, momentum and angular momentum, and every proposed reaction must satisfy all of them.
Doubly magic nuclei such as oxygen-16, with closed proton and neutron shells, show binding energies well above the smooth trend of their neighbours.
Binding energy per nucleon climbs to iron-56 and falls beyond it, which is the whole reason fusion powers stars and fission powers reactors: both release energy by moving matter towards the peak.
conditions: The semi-empirical mass formula is fitted to known nuclei, so its predictions are most reliable in the region where the coefficients were fitted and degrade for exotic nuclei.
Alpha decay proceeds by quantum tunnelling, and the extreme sensitivity of the half-life to the alpha energy and Q-value - the Geiger-Nuttall relation - is the essential experimental handle.
Fission and fusion release energy only because the products sit nearer the peak of the binding-energy curve than the fuel does.
Quasi-stable nuclei are predicted by the liquid-drop model, but shell effects require the nuclear shell model, and neither is exact.
The liquid-drop model gets nuclear masses roughly right but misses the shell and pairing effects that explain the magic numbers and the fine structure of fission barriers.

mysteries.question: What is the neutrino's mass?
mysteries.note: The US Department of Energy reported KATRIN's direct upper bound of 0.45 eV/c^2 in 2026; the exact value remains unknown.

mysteries.question: How strong are the shell effects that make magic nuclei so stable?
mysteries.note: Magic numbers are firmly established experimentally, but their quantitative origin in the nucleon-nucleon interaction remains a subtle many-body problem.

mysteries.question: What is the internal structure of the neutron?
mysteries.note: The neutron is not a point particle, and its charge and magnetic structure is being probed at accelerators and in precision atomic-physics experiments.

units.summary: Solid-state physics explains why metals conduct and insulators do not, why semiconductors conduct better when heated and metals worse, and why resistance can vanish altogether below a critical temperature.
facts: In a solid, allowed energy levels broaden into bands; overlapping bands make a metal, while a gap between the valence and conduction bands makes a semiconductor or an insulator.
In a metal the conductivity falls as temperature rises because more scattering; in a semiconductor it rises because more carriers are excited across the gap.
The Fermi level sits at the top of the occupied states at 0 K in a metal, and the Fermi energy of copper is about 7 eV.
Carrier concentration in a semiconductor follows n proportional to T^(3/2) exp(-Eg/2kT), so the temperature dependence is exponential and steep.
Doping shifts the Fermi level and produces n-type or p-type material; the band gap itself is unchanged by doping.
Below the critical temperature a superconductor has exactly zero resistance and expels magnetic fields (the Meissner effect); BCS theory explains conventional superconductors through Cooper pairs.
The band structure is one object that explains whether a solid conducts, whether it is a semiconductor, and whether it becomes superconducting when it gets cold.
conditions: Band theory assumes a periodic potential, so it describes crystals well and amorphous or strongly disordered materials poorly.
BCS theory accounts for conventional phonon-mediated superconductors but not the high-temperature cuprates, for which a complete microscopic understanding is still outstanding.
Superconductivity requires all three of T below T_c, current density below the critical value, and field below the critical field.
The temperature dependence of a semiconductor is exponential only in the extrinsic or intrinsic regimes described by the model; heavy doping and high fields break that description.
The nearly-free-electron model treats the ions as a periodic potential and the electrons as free particles; it breaks down for narrow bands, strong correlations and the high-temperature cuprates.

mysteries.question: What is the microscopic mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates?
mysteries.note: The US Department of Energy notes that a complete understanding of these newer materials remains an outstanding problem.

mysteries.question: Can the critical temperature of a superconductor be predicted from its structure and composition?
mysteries.note: Deliberately doping a material has raised its critical temperature, and ORNL reports advances in hunting better superconducting materials, but reliable prediction remains out of reach.

units.summary: The final unit is about the edge of the subject: the Standard Model and where it stops, the detection of gravitational waves and neutrino oscillations, and the questions that a generation of experiments is now narrowing - slowly, and honestly.
facts: The Standard Model describes the particles and forces that have been confirmed in the laboratory, but it does not explain dark matter, dark energy, quantum gravity, or the cosmic matter-antimatter imbalance.

The LHCb collaboration at CERN observed CP violation in baryon decays - announced in March 2025 and published in Nature in July 2025 - adding a piece to the matter-antimatter puzzle, though the Standard Model's CP violation remains far too small to explain the observed imbalance (CERN).
The Higgs field gives mass to the W and Z bosons and to fermions through the Yukawa coupling, and the Higgs boson was observed at the LHC in 2012.
Neutrino oscillation proved that neutrinos have mass, which reshaped how the Standard Model is interpreted.
Gravitational waves were first detected in 2015 by LIGO, opening a new observational window on the universe.
Experiments in the frontier are statements of probability with controlled systematics: evidence means a statistically significant deviation, not proof.
The Standard Model accounts for three of the four forces and every confirmed particle, but not dark matter, dark energy, quantum gravity, or the matter-antimatter asymmetry.
conditions: Every frontier claim carries an uncertainty; a null result constrains the strength of a coupling rather than proving absence.
The Standard Model is an effective description validated at the energies tested, and new physics could appear above them without invalidating it.
Numerical simulation is a third pillar of the subject, and it must be validated against analytically solvable limits and against experiment.
Observational limits and theoretical predictions live on different timescales; a bound announced by an experiment can tighten long before a theory explains it.
The Higgs field gives mass to the W and Z bosons and to the fermions, but most of the mass of everyday matter comes from the binding energy inside protons and neutrons, not from the Higgs.

mysteries.question: Why is there far more matter than antimatter in the universe?
mysteries.note: CP violation is necessary but, in the Standard Model, far too small; mechanisms such as leptogenesis are candidate explanations under active study (CERN).

mysteries.question: What drives the accelerating expansion of the universe?
mysteries.note: The observations are secure; the mechanism is not, and no confirmed detection of the responsible particle has been made.

mysteries.question: Does gravity admit a consistent quantum description?
mysteries.note: No fully consistent theory exists, and the attempts to build one have not yet produced testable predictions.
